title: The wild man by the river (Mark 1:4–8)
word: The wild man by the river
hook: John the Baptist in camel hair calls people to turn around

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy in the temple, found asking questions. Your line was questions belong in the temple. What did you finally ask? Now the story jumps about eighteen years. Day forty-seven.

Imagine a man living outside town, in the wild. He wears rough clothes woven from camel hair, with a leather belt. He eats what he can find: locusts and wild honey. No house, no title, no invitation. And crowds walk out of the city to hear him. Mark's Gospel doesn't open with a manger. It opens here, in the desert by the Jordan River, with this man shouting. His name is John, and people will call him John the Baptist. Mark says the whole region of Judea went out to him, and people from Jerusalem too. What was he saying that was worth the walk? Today, the wild man by the river.
screen: `CAMEL HAIR AND A LEATHER BELT.` → `LOCUSTS AND WILD HONEY.` → `CROWDS WALK OUT TO HEAR HIM.`

segments.voice: Mark begins with a line from the prophet Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." Then: "John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins." Repentance is a heavy church word. Here's what's inside it. The Greek is metanoia: meta, change, and noia, from the word for mind. A change of mind. The Hebrew prophets used a simpler word, shuv: turn around, go back. So when John preaches repentance, the picture isn't mainly groveling. It's a person walking the wrong way who stops, turns, and heads home. Then he washes them in the river. Water had long been used in Jewish life for washing and becoming clean, and John makes it a sign of a fresh start. And his clothes are a message too: the Bible describes the prophet Elijah the same way, hairy, with a leather belt. People would have noticed. But the most surprising thing is what John says about himself: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose." Untying sandals was a servant's job. John has crowds, fame, a following, and he spends it all pointing past himself. I baptize you with water, he says. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. John's whole job is to get people turned around and facing the right way, so they'll recognize the one who's coming. A Jewish historian of the time, Josephus, remembered him too, as a good man who called people to live justly.
screen: `A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `METANOIA: A CHANGE OF MIND.` · `SHUV: TURN AROUND, GO BACK.` · `NOT WORTHY TO UNTIE HIS SANDALS.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle in, and breathe slowly. Now think about direction, not guilt. Is there one small thing you keep walking toward that takes you somewhere you don't want to go? A habit, a tone of voice with someone, a scroll at midnight, a grudge. Something small enough to name. Just name it, quietly. Then picture yourself stopping, and turning around. Not a big dramatic scene. Just a turn. If you pray, you can ask for help turning. The bell holds the time.
The wild man by the river. John the Baptist, in camel hair, calling crowds to turn around, and pointing past himself to someone greater.
screen: `THE WILD MAN BY THE RIVER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: turn around. start again. Today, when you catch yourself heading toward the thing you named, just turn. As many times as it takes. Day forty-seven.

howItsDone: Many Christians remember John the Baptist during Advent, the weeks before Christmas, when his call to prepare the way is read in church. His birth is celebrated on June 24, and in many traditions repentance is practiced through confession, private or shared, and a fresh start.

original.note: Greek: repentance. Meta, change, and noia, from the word for mind: a change of mind, a turning around.

trapdoor: what you thought: repent means feel terrible about yourself.
what it means: stop, turn around, and start again, facing the right way.
what a scholar hears: the Greek metanoia is a change of mind, and behind it stands the Hebrew prophets' shuv, to turn back, the root of teshuvah, the Jewish word for repentance.

notes: 'About eighteen years' between Luke 2:42 (age twelve) and Luke 3:23 (about thirty); approximate.
Metanoia etymology: meta + nous (mind); the script says 'noia, from the word for mind'. Confirm the simplification.
Hebrew shuv (שׁוּב) and teshuvah; confirm the link as phrased.
Jewish ritual washing (immersion for purity) as background to John's baptism; kept general.
Elijah's description: 2 Kings 1:8 ('an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather').
Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.2, describes John as a good man who exhorted Jews to practice virtue and justice; paraphrased.
Nativity of John the Baptist, June 24 (Western calendar).
